solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Killer’s dossier, one detectives fill in

definitions.note: a filicide is both the act and the person who kills their own child

indicators.note: to fill in is to occupy the inside of something, so these pieces go inside another

blocks.note: a dossier is a file of documents
the Roman numeral for one
the Criminal Investigation Department, the British police detective branch

explanation.surface: A murderer's case file, which a squad of detectives is completing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fill in' reads as completing a form, but it puts letters inside the dossier. CID is the detective branch of British police forces.
explanation.definitionFit: Like homicide, the word names both the crime and its perpetrator, here a parent who kills their own child.

clue.text: Frequency with which sect members go hungry

blocks.note: F is the standard abbreviation for frequency
the Amish are a plain-living Anabaptist sect

explanation.surface: A question about how often members of a religious group fast.
explanation.walkthrough: The Amish are a Christian sect in North America known for simple living; 'with which' simply joins the pieces to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To famish is to suffer extreme hunger or starve, a slightly old-fashioned verb.

clue.text: Cat that’s trapped a rook’s airway

indicators.note: a trap catches and holds its prey inside, so one piece encloses the others

blocks.note: the lynx is a wild cat
taken as written
R is the chess notation for a rook

explanation.surface: A cat has caught a bird and is now gripping its windpipe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rook' suggests the bird, which fits the hunting picture, but it is the chess piece, abbreviated R.
explanation.definitionFit: The larynx, or voice box, sits at the top of the windpipe and forms part of the respiratory passage.

clue.text: Naïve Democrat taken in by cool president

indicators.note: to be taken in is to be admitted inside, so one piece is held within another

blocks.note: to cool something is to chill it
D is the abbreviation for a Democrat in US politics
Ike was the nickname of President Eisenhower

explanation.surface: A gullible member of one party is fooled by a laid-back leader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cool president' reads as one laid-back leader, but the adjective is a verb here and the president is Eisenhower by his nickname.
explanation.definitionFit: Being naïve means having the trusting innocence typical of a young child.

clue.text: It’s in black and white, you can check on it

definitions.text: It’s in black and white, you can check on it

blocks.clueFragment: It’s in black and white, you can check on it
blocks.note: surface reading: a printed document whose facts you may verify

blocks.clueFragment: It’s in black and white, you can check on it
blocks.note: setter's reading: a chequered playing surface of dark and light squares on which you move pieces

explanation.walkthrough: 'In black and white' usually means written down, and 'check' means verify; here the colours are literal squares and 'check' hints at chequers. Draughts is the British name for checkers.
explanation.definitionFit: The board for checkers is a grid of alternating dark and light squares, so it literally is chequered black and white.

clue.text: Jokes about cutting prices

indicators.note: something that cuts into another goes inside it, dividing it

blocks.note: C stands for circa, Latin for about
fares are the prices charged for travel

explanation.surface: Mockery of reductions in what things cost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cutting prices' reads as a discount, but cutting here means splitting the word for prices with the single letter for about.
explanation.definitionFit: A farce is something absurd or laughable, and in plural can mean mockeries or jokes.

clue.text: Argonaut dropping gun parts off vessel

indicators.note: dropping something means letting it fall away, so those letters are removed
something off has gone wrong or awry, so the remaining letters are disordered

blocks.note: taken as written
the separate letters of the word gun, scattered through the first word

explanation.surface: One of Jason's crew throws pieces of his weapon over the side of his ship.
explanation.walkthrough: The Argonauts sailed with Jason in the Argo. Removing G, U and N from ARGONAUT leaves AROAT, which is rearranged. 'Vessel' suggests the ship, but it is a blood vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: The aorta is the main artery leaving the heart, the largest blood vessel in the body.

clue.text: Top part covering Aintree’s second horse jump

indicators.note: second points to the letter in position two of the word
a covering wraps round what it covers, so one piece goes around another

blocks.note: a cap is a top or lid
an actor's part is a role
the second letter of the racecourse's name

explanation.surface: Describes the highest section of a famous obstacle at a racecourse.
explanation.walkthrough: Aintree is the Liverpool course where the Grand National steeplechase is run, which makes 'horse jump' look like a fence there; 'second' wants a horse finishing second, but it picks a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A capriole is a dressage leap in which the horse jumps vertically and kicks out its hind legs.

clue.text: Strips of light paper with black plastic seam

indicators.note: plastic material can be moulded into any shape, so these letters are remoulded

blocks.note: The Sun is a British tabloid newspaper
B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils
taken as written

explanation.surface: Describes thin strips of lightweight paper joined with a dark plastic seam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strips of light paper' wants to be one phrase about thin paper, but the definition ends at 'light' and 'paper' is a newspaper. The Sun is a UK daily tabloid.
explanation.definitionFit: Sunbeams are narrow rays or shafts of sunlight, which can be pictured as strips.

clue.text: Old lady managed to swallow fly in a layer of cake

indicators.note: what is swallowed ends up inside the swallower, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: an old lady is slang for one's mother, hence ma
to manage a business is to run it
a trouser fly is fastened with a zip

explanation.surface: Evokes the nursery rhyme about the old lady who swallowed a fly, here hidden in a cake.
explanation.walkthrough: The rhyme makes the fly an insect, but it is the opening on trousers; 'old lady' is British slang for mother.
explanation.definitionFit: Marzipan, an almond paste, is rolled out as the layer under the icing on fruit cakes.

clue.text: Old head saw parent after work

indicators.note: once something has been worked on it is reshaped, so the letters come out in new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A former headteacher spotted a pupil's mother or father once the working day was over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old head saw' reads as a retired head teacher seeing someone, but 'saw' is a noun, a cutting tool used on the skull.
explanation.definitionFit: A trepan is an early surgical instrument, a cylindrical saw for boring holes in the skull, now replaced by the trephine.

clue.text: Ride or cycle in tight skirt

blocks.note: tight and merry are both mild slang for tipsy
to skirt something is to go round it

explanation.surface: A choice between riding a horse or a bike wearing a close-fitting skirt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tight skirt' looks like clothing, but tight means drunk and skirt is a verb meaning to pass around the edge.
explanation.definitionFit: A carousel is a fairground ride, and figuratively an endless whirl of repeating activity, a cycle.

clue.text: Church group’s crime not even reported

indicators.note: something reported is passed on by word of mouth, so we want how words sound

blocks.note: a crime is a sin, and a number not even is odd

explanation.surface: A church council's wrongdoing has not even made the news.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not even' reads as 'not so much as', but it means odd, the opposite of an even number.
explanation.definitionFit: A synod is an assembly of clergy and church officials that governs church affairs.

clue.text: Pineapple rings in syrup

indicators.note: to ring something is to encircle it, so one piece goes around the other

blocks.note: pineapple is old military slang for a hand grenade, from its segmented shape
taken as written

explanation.surface: Tinned pineapple rings packed in sugary liquid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pineapple rings' is the tinned fruit, but rings is a verb, and the pineapple is a hand grenade.
explanation.definitionFit: Grenadine is a sweet red cordial originally made from pomegranate, used in cocktails.

clue.text: Champion, one with a prize fruit

blocks.note: a champion is the victor
the Roman numeral for one
taken as written
a plum job or role is a prize one

explanation.surface: A winner at a show, someone who has grown prize-winning produce.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prize fruit' reads as one phrase, but prize is an adjective meaning choice, like a plum posting.
explanation.definitionFit: The Victoria is a popular English variety of plum, red and sweet, an example of a fruit.

clue.text: Plant from India I set up in water

indicators.note: in a down clue going up means reading from the bottom, back to front
in places these pieces inside another

blocks.note: I is India in the NATO phonetic alphabet
taken as written
to set, like a jelly, is to gel
aqua is Latin for water

explanation.surface: A plant brought over from India and grown hydroponically.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From India' suggests where the plant originates, but India is a single letter from the phonetic alphabet; in this down clue 'up' turns the following pair over.
explanation.definitionFit: Aquilegia is the botanical name for columbine, a flowering garden plant.

clue.text: Bar starts to deep-fry its pasty

indicators.note: starts are the opening letters, so only the first of each word counts

blocks.note: the first letters of the two words
pasty as an adjective describes a pale, sallow complexion

explanation.surface: A pub that serves a deep-fried pasty, a Cornish pie.
explanation.walkthrough: A Cornish pasty is a British pastry pie, so 'pasty' looks like food; here it is the adjective for a pale, unhealthy face, and 'Bar' is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To bar something is to forbid or prohibit it, which is what disallowing does.

clue.text: Tart shop’s beginning to advertise

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word
to trumpet something is to proclaim it loudly

explanation.surface: A bakery's opening offer is to promote its pastries.
explanation.walkthrough: In a shop setting 'Tart' looks like a pastry, but it is the slang word for a promiscuous woman.
explanation.definitionFit: Strumpet and tart are both dated, derogatory slang terms for a promiscuous woman or prostitute.

clue.text: Eventually got from home to Marathon?

definitions.note: a phrase describing how the journey was made, not a synonym

blocks.note: first meaning: over a long period, in the end
second meaning, whimsically: travelled the distance to the Greek town on foot over a great distance

explanation.walkthrough: The marathon race takes its name from the run from Marathon to Athens; the question mark flags the playful literal reading.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means ultimately, after a long time, which is what eventually expresses.

clue.text: Some feel too pumped up to travel leisurely

indicators.note: some means a portion only, so the letters are a run within the words
in a down clue going up means the letters read from bottom to top

blocks.note: the run of letters across the ends of these words

explanation.surface: Some people are too excited to take a slow, relaxed trip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pumped up' reads as excited, but 'up' is the reversal in this down clue. Pootle is British slang for moving along in a leisurely way.
explanation.definitionFit: To pootle is to amble or drive along slowly and without hurry, informal British usage.

clue.text: Grand artist frames something attractive

indicators.note: a frame surrounds a picture, so one piece goes around another

blocks.note: G is short for grand, a thousand
Édouard Manet was a French painter

explanation.surface: A great painter puts a lovely work into a frame.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grand artist' reads as a great painter, but grand is G and the artist is Manet.
explanation.definitionFit: A magnet attracts iron, and figuratively anything that draws people in is a magnet.

clue.text: One scoring away from home?

blocks.note: surface reading: a footballer who gets a goal at an away fixture
setter's reading: someone who has sexual conquests outside their marriage

explanation.walkthrough: The sporting sense of scoring an away goal is the decoy; in slang scoring means getting lucky in bed, and home means the marriage.
explanation.definitionFit: A married person who sleeps with someone other than their spouse is unfaithful outside the marital home.

clue.text: Keynote article made less commercial

indicators.note: less means minus, so letters are taken away

blocks.note: the definite article
taken as written
an ad is a commercial

explanation.surface: A newspaper's lead piece toned down its advertising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Made less commercial' reads as one phrase, but it means MADE with AD removed, leaving ME.
explanation.definitionFit: A keynote is the central idea or main point, the same as a theme.

clue.text: Start off haughty meeting a cleaner

indicators.note: with its start off, a word loses its first letter

blocks.note: aloof means distant and haughty
taken as written

explanation.surface: Begin with a snooty attitude when introduced to a cleaning lady.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cleaner' suggests a person who cleans; it is a bath sponge. The answer is the variant spelling of loofah.
explanation.definitionFit: A loofa is the dried fibrous fruit of a gourd used as a scrubbing sponge, so a cleaner.

clue.text: Cut that’s bound to include page five hundred

indicators.note: to include something is to take it inside

blocks.note: to lope is to run with long bounding strides
P is the abbreviation for page
D is the Roman numeral for five hundred

explanation.surface: An edited cut of a book that is sure to run to five hundred pages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bound' suggests a bound book or certainty, but it is a verb meaning leap.
explanation.definitionFit: To lop is to chop off a branch or limb, so lopped means cut off, past tense.

clue.text: Metal cask to hold gent’s rum

indicators.note: rum is British slang for odd or strange, so the letters come out peculiar

blocks.note: a tun is a large cask for wine or beer
taken as written without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A metal barrel to store a gentleman's rum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rum' reads as the spirit, which fits the cask, but it is the adjective meaning strange.
explanation.definitionFit: Tungsten is a hard, dense metallic element, used for lamp filaments.

clue.text: Operated on ram with anaesthetic

blocks.note: W is the abbreviation for with
ether was an early general anaesthetic

explanation.surface: A vet performed surgery on a sheep after putting it under.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Operated on' reads as a verb in a sentence, but the whole phrase is a noun: a ram that has had an operation.
explanation.definitionFit: A wether is a castrated male sheep, so it is a ram that has had surgery.

clue.text: Social worker carrying record player to a church next-door

indicators.note: to carry is to hold within, so one piece surrounds the others

blocks.note: ants are social insects, and a worker is a caste of ant
a disc jockey plays records
taken as written
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A welfare officer lugs a turntable to the church beside her office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Social worker' is a job title, but here it is an insect; 'record player' is not a turntable but a disc jockey. CE is the Church of England.
explanation.definitionFit: Adjacent means lying beside or neighbouring, the same as next-door used as an adjective.
